title: The Victorian with Too Many Windows
premise: A building adds one window whenever a secret is spoken nearby.
pressure: An Old Town Victorian grows another window every time someone admits a secret. The owner has put up a confession-tour booth, complete with souvenir keys. Upstairs, a tenant says strangers have begun paying to peer into her bedroom. 'He calls it heritage tourism,' she says. 'I call it Tuesday.' The owner offers you a free ticket if you can coax out one more confession.
investigate: Count the added windows against permits, without asking anyone for a confession
success: Your count catches a window that should look onto the neighbor's brick wall. Instead it shows the harbor a decade older, with a rust-red boat absent from today's docks. The tenant permits a photograph of the view, but only after she leaves the frame. The owner offers twice the ticket price for her name. You decline.
failure: The extra window closes before your camera focuses. You cannot prove a thing about its future harbor. The owner immediately tells tourists you witnessed a miracle, using the tenant's address as a selling point. She asks you to correct the story in public, though you know the crowd will remember your name instead of hers.
help: Help the tenant end the invasive tours and reclaim her front steps
helpOutcome: You help the tenants reclaim their steps and block the ticket line with their own front-porch furniture. The owner calls it vandalism. 'We bought the chairs,' the upstairs tenant says. 'They belong in front of our own door.' At dusk the house grows one last window, pointed squarely at the ticket booth.

title: Antique Shop of Almost-Famous Objects
premise: The shop sells history's second-best cursed relics at honest prices.
pressure: An Old Town antique dealer sells objects that nearly became famous: a pen left untouched at a signing, a hat declined by a ghost. A visitor recognizes her grandfather's toolbox in the window and wants it removed before a tour group invents a family scandal.
investigate: Check the toolbox provenance against the shop ledger before trusting its label
success: The listing is wrong, but a receipt bears the date of a future city vote. The dealer preserves the paper as a curiosity and corrects the family's history.
failure: The alleged relic turns out to be a convincing copy. The dealer offers a refund; the visitor still finds her grandfather's repair mark inside the lid.
help: Help the visitor recover the toolbox without making her family story an attraction
helpOutcome: The toolbox goes home and the dealer leaves a blank space in the display. A sign reads NOT FOR SALE, which draws the biggest crowd yet.

title: A Ghost Demands Parking Validation
premise: An Edwardian apparition refuses to haunt without reimbursed meter fees.
pressure: An Edwardian ghost has received a parking ticket under his spectral windshield and refuses to haunt another minute until somebody validates the meter. A city officer wants to tow the invisible car. 'From which end?' asks the tow driver, holding a hook through its bonnet. Two wheelchair users are waiting for the curb space. The ghost insists he was parked here first, which is technically true by eighty-seven years.
investigate: Compare the citation with historic street maps and an actual meter record
success: The citation names a narrow lane paved over decades ago. The ghost wants the historical error to erase his late fee, but the officer points to a perfectly modern curb ramp he has been blocking. You find the old street plan and show both of them. The hearing can proceed tomorrow; tonight the car needs to move. The ghost calls this revisionism and starts his engine.
failure: The ticket turns to lint before you can preserve the number. The ghost claims this proves the city never had jurisdiction; the officer insists the fine doubles. Meanwhile a woman trying to use the ramp asks whether either of them remembers she is here. You cannot settle the old fee. You can make room for her without needing a verdict.
help: Help the people who use the street propose an accessible parking rule
helpOutcome: You help the officer issue a temporary access pass for the ghost's inconveniently old registration, on condition the spectral car stops occupying the curb ramp. He moves it with magnificent offense. The wheelchair users get through, the tow driver goes home, and the ghost says he will haunt city hall instead. 'There's already a waiting list,' the clerk replies.

title: The Postcard from Eureka, Mars
premise: A tourist card shows an accurate street scene under two suns.
pressure: A postcard on the Eureka waterfront shows the town beneath two suns, with the correct shop signs and a tram nobody remembers building. A collector offers the owner three hundred dollars if she signs over all rights to the picture. 'I only wanted to send a card to my brother,' she says. The archivist wants the original for conservation; the collector wants it before anybody notices the street corner has moved.
investigate: Compare the postcard's storefront shadows with today's street layout
success: You compare the double shadows to the real storefronts and find a doorway that appears on the postcard but nowhere on the assessor's plans. The archivist wants to publish the discovery immediately. The owner folds her arms: 'It's still my card.' You preserve the measurements and ask for permission to quote her, rather than turning her family message into a public attraction.
failure: Rain eats the return address before you can make a copy. Two clear circles remain where the suns were printed; the collector declares them proof of Mars and raises his offer. The owner almost sells, needing the money. You cannot prove the postcard's origin or dictate her choice, but you can tell her what the conservator can still save.
help: Ask the owner before donating or publishing somebody else's impossible souvenir
helpOutcome: You help the owner make a time-limited loan agreement with the archive, including the right to take the card back. Neighbors annotate a copy with memories of shops that have closed and places that never existed. The collector calls the arrangement financially foolish. The owner mails her brother a photograph and keeps the original in a dry envelope.

title: The Perilous Plunge into Monday
premise: A costumed jumper emerges from Humboldt Bay on a different day.
place: Eureka F Street waterfront / Perilous Plunge
pressure: A bay-plunge fundraiser jumper comes out of Saturday's water with Monday's newspaper caught in her costume. Her friends want to celebrate the time travel; she wants someone to notice that she is shaking and cannot find her phone.
investigate: Compare the newspaper edition, event video and volunteer check-in times
success: The footage shows two date displays disagreeing while her jump remains continuous. The organizer saves both originals without claiming a scientific breakthrough.
failure: A spectator overwrites the clip with a victory montage. The jumper still has a Monday parking slip stapled to her costume and asks to keep it.
help: Get the jumper dry and ask a medic to check her before the interviews begin
helpOutcome: She warms up under a borrowed blanket and calls home. A fundraiser volunteer labels the newspaper LOST PROPERTY, FUTURE, and takes a lunch break.

title: The Judge Who Is Also an Octopus
premise: A fundraiser award panel has an unusually flexible member.
place: Eureka F Street waterfront / Perilous Plunge
pressure: An octopus in borrowed judicial robes sits on the fundraiser's prize panel. Every arm holds a different scorecard; one scores craftsmanship, one scores charm, and one is giving sixes to everyone it likes. The competing crews have seen this sort of thing from human judges.
investigate: Ask the panel to publish one rule that even an octopus must follow
success: Four arms point to four versions of the same sculpture, each apparently entered under a different year. The fifth holds up a dated ticket from the next fundraiser.
failure: The ink cloud makes the votes illegible. A volunteer saves one dissent in a plastic sleeve, proving at least that the disagreement was real.
help: Invite the competing teams to help set a fair judging process
helpOutcome: The teams settle on visible criteria and agree to share a repair grant instead of declaring the losers defective. The octopus signs with a damp flourish.

title: Best Costume: Unidentified Object
premise: Someone registers as a weather balloon with very convincing paperwork.
place: Eureka F Street waterfront / Perilous Plunge
pressure: A costume competitor has registered as a weather balloon with a laminated certificate, an inspection history and a polite refusal to explain how the zipper works. A volunteer is being asked to disqualify the act or certify an actual unidentified object.
investigate: Compare the permit number with the published costume category rules
success: The form was issued by an office scheduled to open next year. It does not exempt the entrant from today's safety inspection, which everyone accepts.
failure: The stamp bleeds when you try to copy it. The volunteer retains a witness signature and declines to make a ruling based on damp stationery.
help: Help the volunteer judge the costume fairly without demanding the entrant unmask
helpOutcome: The act competes in the open category and the inspection passes. The trophy reads BEST AMBIGUOUS PAPERWORK.

title: The Marching Lumberjack Paradox
premise: A drumbeat repeats yesterday's parade in reverse.
place: Eureka F Street waterfront / Perilous Plunge
pressure: A drumline marches backward along an Old Town block while the rest of the parade insists on going forward. No one is being deliberately rude. One drummer says the tune is tomorrow's; the crossing guard says a collision would be very much today.
investigate: Record the cadence while marking where the two parades physically meet
success: The missing beat spells a street closure scheduled for tomorrow's tide. The crossing guard confirms the street exists and declines to accept instructions from a snare drum.
failure: Your recording catches only applause. A drummer writes the count on the back of your hand and asks you to return the marker when time resumes.
help: Move spectators out of the crossing and give both groups a safe route
helpOutcome: Both marching groups pass safely, and the spectators find somewhere to stand without having to believe in reversible Tuesdays.

title: The Hot Tub Oracle
premise: A post-plunge hot tub provides dubious prophecies in bubbles.
place: Eureka F Street waterfront / Perilous Plunge
pressure: The post-plunge hot tub is delivering prophecies in soap bubbles. Its forecasts keep saving someone's day while assigning the credit to strangers. The exhausted volunteer who filled it is being hailed as a mystic and has not eaten since sunrise.
investigate: Write down a prediction and check how the event was actually documented
success: The forecast accurately warns of a failed heater, but the bubble credits a person who is out of town. You log the repair instead of the legend.
failure: The message bursts before anyone agrees on its wording. A witness remembers the temperature warning, which a technician can verify without an oracle.
help: Make sure the volunteer gets a break and the tub passes its ordinary safety checks
helpOutcome: The heater is shut down, warm drinks appear, and the volunteer gets lunch. The tub insists it predicted the sandwiches.

title: The Oyster Council Convenes
premise: A floating shellfish parliament has issued a subpoena for a gull.
pressure: The Oyster Council is trying a gull for mussel theft on a floating platform in Humboldt Bay. The prosecutor has a pearl necklace and seventeen witnesses who are all the same clam. The gull demands counsel; the harbormaster demands the channel back before a working boat has to turn around. 'Justice takes time,' the oyster speaker declares. 'A fishing boat takes space,' the harbormaster replies.
investigate: Examine the mussel evidence and the parliament's jurisdiction claims
success: You discover the supposed theft coincides with a genuine change in tidal current. The mussels have been moving. The gull calls this exoneration and flies away before anyone can establish its innocence. The harbormaster logs the measured drift, but refuses the Council's demand for a permanent courthouse in the fairway.
failure: The gull eats exhibit B, which may or may not have been an actual mussel. The hearing collapses into accusations. A shellfish grower shows you photographs of the current shift, useful but insufficient to determine guilt. The prosecutor wants a conviction anyway. You can preserve the observation without signing the verdict.
help: Help move the assembly away from boats and let the accused gull depart
helpOutcome: You and two volunteers tow the shell parliament toward a sheltered slip, letting the gull leave without a forced confession. The speaker denounces interference in sovereign proceedings. An exhausted deckhand says the harbor has room for democracy, just not democracy parked in the channel. The oysters adjourn until low tide.

title: The Missing Channel Marker
premise: A navigational buoy goes on strike because the sea keeps lying.
pressure: A channel marker has drifted ashore and drawn a picket line in the sand. It says the chart has been lying about the depth for months. A fishing crew is preparing to take the shortcut it used to mark.
investigate: Compare the buoy's last recorded position with current soundings and chart updates
success: The shortcut has shoaled. A skipper radios the measured position; the buoy's labor claim can wait for daylight.
failure: The tide turns before your sounding settles. A fishing crew shows you the fuel bill for taking the long way; you cannot make that money reappear by calling the shortcut safe. The harbor office keeps your incomplete drift sketch marked provisional. The buoy crosses your name off its picket petition.
help: Warn the crew to use the charted route and support a safe inspection
helpOutcome: The boats take the longer channel without incident. The buoy accepts a dry place to rest and a temporary sign reading STRIKE, NOT NAVIGATION.

title: Submarine with Bicycle Pedals
premise: A homemade contraption claims to be a federally funded research craft.
pressure: A pedal-powered submarine advertises itself as federally funded research. The crew is three sleepless mechanics and a child assigned to keep the clipboard dry. The tide is rising and the craft's hatch can only be opened from outside.
investigate: Read the grant paperwork and test the hatch before anybody boards
success: The grant letter carries the seal of a department that will not exist until after a future storm. You log it as a mystery and the hatch as a present-tense problem.
failure: Water enters during the unmanned test. The mechanics record the leak without excuses; the child triumphantly writes NO PASSENGERS beside the result.
help: Move the demonstration ashore and give the child a safe role
helpOutcome: The crew pedals the submarine on blocks, to great applause, and posts a list of repairs before its first proper launch. Nobody becomes a research subject.

title: The Tide Returns a Bicycle
premise: A rustless bike carries evidence of a trip nobody remembers.
pressure: The tide returns a bicycle without a fleck of rust. Its rental tag records a ride out to a pier that no longer exists, and the rental clerk is afraid the owner will charge her for a vehicle she never signed out.
investigate: Match the tag number to the rental records and surviving pier maps
success: The trip date is tomorrow; a photographed frame number matches the present bike. The clerk logs it as evidence rather than charging a customer.
failure: Saltwater ruins the QR code as you scan it. The paper key tag survives with the initials of someone the clerk remembers.
help: Help the clerk keep the bicycle safe and correct the inventory without blame
helpOutcome: The shop locks the bike inside and writes an incident note. Somebody hangs a HELMET REQUIRED sign on the door to the past.

title: The Redwood's Lost-and-Found
premise: A park bench collects small things that people forgot as children.
pressure: A redwood-park bench is holding lost childhood belongings: a mitten, a model airplane, a letter never mailed. One item makes a visitor go still. The caretaker has been ordered to remove the bench because nobody filed the proper installation permit.
investigate: Check where the bench came from and ask before identifying anyone's belongings
success: An old maintenance ledger records its arrival tomorrow. The caretaker preserves the entry, and the visitor quietly claims the letter without having to explain it.
failure: The bench's plaque becomes unreadable under your camera. You still find a municipal bolt mark beneath the seat and report it as a trace.
help: Help the caretaker catalog the items privately while the bench is evaluated
helpOutcome: The objects are stored with consent and the visitor chooses which one to keep. The bench stays another week, pending a very ordinary hearing.

title: The Volunteer in the Bear Costume
premise: The person giving animal talks cannot take off their costume.
pressure: A volunteer at the zoo gives a flawless habitat lecture in a bear costume he cannot remove. 'The children think it's adorable,' he says. 'I haven't slept without a mascot head in three months.' The bear's second voice corrects his taxonomy from somewhere inside the padding. A manager suggests filming an interview for publicity. The volunteer asks you not to let that happen.
investigate: With his permission, examine the seam and ask when the corrections began
success: With his permission, you find a lining label dated next year stitched into fabric bought three seasons ago. The keeper confirms both dates; neither tells you how to unfasten it. The voice inside the head says, 'Habitat destruction,' then gently corrects itself to, 'Personal boundaries.' The volunteer laughs at the distinction until he nearly cries.
failure: The zipper breaks in your hands, making the costume harder to open. The volunteer tries to joke about being a lifelong bear. You apologize instead of calling it a lucky clue and ask for a proper seamstress. The manager complains about closing the exhibit; the keeper cancels the next talk anyway.
help: Ask a seamstress and the keeper to arrange a private, safe way out
helpOutcome: You close the viewing area and let the seamstress work without an audience. When the volunteer finally sits in ordinary clothes, the bear head tells the keeper to install a drinking fountain. The keeper promises to consider it. The volunteer says the next lecture can be delivered by somebody who volunteered for it.

title: A Peacock with a Search Warrant
premise: An extremely official bird investigates missing color.
pressure: A peacock with a paper badge serves a search warrant on the zoo's missing colors. Painted signs have gone white overnight, and the bird insists on confiscating every pencil. The keepers would like the animals' enclosures explained to visitors before noon.
investigate: Read the warrant with a keeper and compare the signs with old maintenance records
success: A transfer slip for the missing pigment bears a date from a future conservation exhibit. The keeper copies the number; the peacock keeps insisting it has jurisdiction.
failure: The peacock seizes your pencil before you finish the list. A keeper has already photographed the blank signs and lends you another one.
help: Help restore legible visitor signs while leaving the animals undisturbed
helpOutcome: Keepers and visitors repaint the wayfinding signs from safe references. The peacock awards the staff his badge, which is made of a very ordinary leaf.

title: The Picnic That Never Ends
premise: One family has been packing up the same picnic for decades.
pressure: A family picnic has lasted long enough for three generations of children to keep arriving after the blanket is folded. The grandparents are exhausted and one child needs medication from the car. A photographer thinks the whole thing would make a charming brochure.
investigate: Compare the family's photos and dates without separating anyone from the table
success: A photograph shows an extra place setting before its occupant was born. The family keeps the original and lets you record only the date discrepancy.
failure: You lose track of the sequence halfway through. The youngest child has written everyone's name on a paper plate, which is at least a reliable headcount.
help: Help the family get necessities and protect their privacy while they leave
helpOutcome: They pack food, medication and children in that order. For the first time the blanket folds flat; nobody volunteers it for a museum.

title: The Tree That Grows Entrances
premise: A hollow trunk offers three doors, none requiring a key.
pressure: A hollow redwood presents three doors: PUBLIC, PRIVATE and FORGOTTEN. A ranger says they all lead out, but visitors have been leaving through places they never entered. A school group is approaching, and the PUBLIC door has begun charging admission.
investigate: Check the doorways from outside and compare the ranger's visitor count
success: A carved mark links the PRIVATE exit to a locked maintenance path. The ranger closes the route until its real safety can be checked.
failure: The doors swap labels when you blink. The group's teacher records the original positions, and you agree not to test the unknown exit with children.
help: Help the ranger redirect visitors onto the marked, accessible trail
helpOutcome: The group sees the living redwood without buying a ticket to anywhere. The PUBLIC door displays a complaint about lost revenue.
